# W2 vs 1099 Take-Home Pay: Which Actually Pays More in 2026?

It's a common dilemma: A company offers you a role and says, "We can bring you on as a W2 employee at $80,000, or as a 1099 contractor at $90,000. Your choice."

$90,000 is bigger than $80,000. So the 1099 offer is better, right? 

**Wrong.** In almost every scenario, the $80k W2 offer will put more money in your pocket and offer better financial security. Let's break down the math to understand why 1099 income is so much more expensive to maintain.

## The Self-Employment Tax Trap

The biggest difference between W2 and 1099 workers is how FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare) are handled.

As a **W2 Employee**, FICA tax is 15.3% total. But your employer pays half (7.65%), and you pay half (7.65%). It comes out of your paycheck automatically.

As a **1099 Contractor**, you are both the employer *and* the employee. That means you have to pay the entire 15.3% yourself. This is known as the Self-Employment Tax. 

*   **W2 FICA on $80k**: $6,120
*   **1099 FICA on $90k**: ~$12,716

Instantly, that extra $10,000 you were offered as a contractor is almost entirely wiped out by the extra FICA taxes.

## The Hidden Costs of 1099 Work

Taxes are just the beginning. When you are a W2 employee, your compensation package includes benefits that have real monetary value. As a 1099 contractor, you have to buy these yourself with after-tax dollars.

1.  **Health Insurance**: Employer-sponsored plans are heavily subsidized. Buying your own comparable plan on the open market can easily cost $400 - $800+ per month.
2.  **Paid Time Off (PTO)**: If a W2 employee takes two weeks of vacation and is sick for 5 days, they still get paid. If a 1099 contractor takes 3 weeks off, they earn $0 during that time. To compare salaries accurately, you have to reduce the 1099 expected income by 6-10% to account for unpaid time off.
3.  **Retirement Matches**: Many W2 jobs offer a 401(k) match (free money). Contractors have to fund their entire retirement via a [Solo 401(k) or SEP IRA](/sep-ira-solo-401k-guide-2026) out of their own pocket.

## The One Advantage of 1099: Write-Offs

It's not all doom and gloom for contractors. The one major advantage 1099 workers have is the ability to deduct business expenses.

If you have to buy a $2,000 laptop, pay for software subscriptions, use a portion of your home as an office, or drive to client sites, you can deduct these expenses from your income before calculating taxes. Furthermore, contractors may qualify for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction, which can shield up to 20% of profits from federal income tax.

## The 30% Rule

A good rule of thumb when comparing offers is the **30% Rule**. 

To have the same standard of living and take-home pay, a 1099 contractor rate needs to be roughly **25% to 30% higher** than a W2 salary offer.

If the W2 offer is $80,000, the 1099 offer shouldn't be $90,000. It needs to be closer to **$104,000** to actually break even after self-employment taxes, health insurance, and unpaid time off.
